Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• 4–5-day worsening of widespread pruritic, erythematous, dry rash on chest, arms, hands, and antecubital fossae; skin cracking but no weeping.  
• Known history of atopic dermatitis; current topical hydrocortisone and emollients no longer adequate.  
• No systemic symptoms (fever, joint pain); no new medications; no drug allergies; intermittent asthma stable.

Working diagnosis  
• Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare—high likelihood based on chronic history and classic flexural distribution.

Relevant differentials (consistent with DDx)  
• Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis—medium likelihood; sudden severe flare could reflect new exposure although patient reports no change.  
• Scabies infestation—low–medium likelihood; pruritus and flexural involvement but lacks burrows, nocturnal itching, or contact cases.

Management  
• Prescribed stronger topical steroid: Betnovate (betamethasone valerate 0.1%) thin layer twice daily × 2 weeks.  
• Prescribed oral antihistamine: Fexofenadine.  
• Continue regular emollients (Diprobase, Dermol).  
• Safety-netting: return if worsening, adverse reaction, or no improvement in 2 weeks.  
• No investigations ordered at this visit; physical examination limited by telehealth.

Health Promotion & Planning

- Education on chronic disease prevention and lifestyle modification:  Advised continued liberal use of emollients; brief instruction on correct fingertip-unit application of topical steroid. Additional preventive counselling not recorded.
- Patient health goals and priorities:  Relief of itching and rash; avoid flare escalation.
- Eligibility for GP Management Plan (GPMP) or Team Care Arrangements (TCA):  Not recorded.

- Follow-up and recall appointments scheduled:  Review via telehealth or in person in 2 weeks, or sooner if deterioration.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Atopic dermatitis flare – High likelihood: chronic condition with classic distribution and symptoms; current topical regimen insufficient.  
2. Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis – Medium likelihood: acute worsening could follow new exposure despite no reported changes.  
3. Scabies infestation – Low–Medium likelihood: intense pruritus in flexural areas but lacks burrows, nocturnal pattern, or household spread.
